# 📜 Bankruptcy Creditor Rights | Wednesday, June 03, 2026

## Analysis & Developments

Today's dominant delta is the Supreme Court's denial of certiorari in the Georgia-Pacific "Texas Two-Step" proceeding, leaving intact the Third Circuit's framework for divisional merger–based mass-tort bankruptcies and resetting the creditor-rights battleground squarely in the district and bankruptcy courts rather than Washington. Simultaneously, Impac Mortgage Holdings, Inc. secured confirmation of its Chapter 11 plan in the Central District of California, and Bestar Inc. obtained Chapter 15 recognition in a cross-border proceeding — two data points that underscore the continued high throughput of consumer-finance and manufacturing restructurings through mid-2026. Against that backdrop, practitioners tracking the Section 548 fraudulent-transfer and equitable-mootness doctrines must recalibrate based on the Court's silence: the "two-step" architecture remains available, but post-confirmation appellate review is increasingly narrowed by mootness doctrine applied with renewed rigor in the Fourth and Third Circuits.

---

### I. Supreme Court Denies Certiorari in Georgia-Pacific Two-Step — Doctrinal Implications for Mass-Tort Creditors

The Supreme Court declined to hear the challenge to Georgia-Pacific LLC's subsidiary-bankruptcy maneuver — the so-called "Texas Two-Step" — confirming the denial of certiorari in *In re Bestwall LLC*, No. 17-31795 (Bankr. W.D.N.C., Chief Judge J. Craig Whitley), an asbestos-liability spin-off case that has been pending in Charlotte since November 2017 (__[Reuters — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivgFBVV95cUxOazJqbzVwTWlFV2N2UXhCYmFKT1dnVHh5WTZCXzlOV3ZRRDhTLUhFRFhHNm9ieXMyanBZQ05xNXF2Q3lqYnY4TExJeXI5akNEN29xemZDbHpJZGxERTJIdmpWNG5KalRRRExfandSV21oYkdSakFmTGV0REFMQWVMVmJTV3E5TGRLV2JZY19vZ3JpNTJzTU1TQnU3ZDNveGhXV3I5cHpxOXp0NWN4R3ZpcU5ZaVA5ak9sNkxZN253)__; __[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__; __[Bloomberg Law — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxNMW91bHpZSHEzb3Z0RVZ5clNiVDhrbjg1YXBuT2h5WEVJaU5UNUFILUhVdnFoQUp2LTF5Z1BJcjVUV0xkMXU4bnlyTmJjTEl4OWM3ZmgyM3NaQmdyc3VmaVBHUDliMkp2bXZ0TkpzSnZWeHpLOEZuNVJoOF9rUjh0Wm00WnVnWVdvcUpITnZUV2s5UGRMR01OZHAxbGsyZXhuM3YzaVVzeVpvUQ)__).

**What the cert denial does — and does not — do.** The denial is not a ruling on the merits of the two-step's legality under 11 U.S.C. §§ 105(a), 1129, or the fraudulent-transfer provisions of § 548. It leaves in place the Western District of North Carolina's jurisdiction over Bestwall and, more consequentially, signals that the Third Circuit's divided 2024 panel ruling in *LTL Management LLC v. Those Parties Listed on Appendix A to Complaint*, No. 23-1835 (3d Cir., panel including Judges Shwartz, Matey, and Roth) — which dismissed LTL Management's second bankruptcy petition for lack of "good faith" financial distress under § 1112(b) — stands as controlling law within the Third Circuit's geographic footprint (__[Bloomberg Law — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxNMW91bHpZSHEzb3Z0RVZ5clNiVDhrbjg1YXBuT2h5WEVJaU5UNUFILUhVdnFoQUp2LTF5Z1BJcjVUV0xkMXU4bnlyTmJjTEl4OWM3ZmgyM3NaQmdyc3VmaVBHUDliMkp2bXZ0TkpzSnZWeHpLOEZuNVJoOF9rUjh0Wm00WnVnWVdvcUpITnZUV2s5UGRMR01OZHAxbGsyZXhuM3YzaVVzeVpvUQ)__).

**The circuit split that now hardens.** The Fourth Circuit (Bestwall's home) has not yet ruled definitively on whether a financially healthy parent may engineer a subsidiary to hold tort liabilities and then file that subsidiary in bankruptcy, depriving tort plaintiffs of jury trials. With the Supreme Court's exit, the Fourth Circuit's eventual ruling in Bestwall — if asbestos claimants there ultimately secure a reviewable adverse ruling on the § 524(g) channeling injunction — becomes the next inflection point. Practitioners should note that the § 524(g) channeling injunction requires, among other things, that the trust hold at least 50% of its voting securities for the benefit of present and future demands; the Bestwall trust funding negotiation remains unresolved after more than eight years. The Court's cert denial extends that uncertainty indefinitely for the approximately 60,000 pending asbestos claimants (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__).

**Creditor-side positioning post-cert denial.** Mass-tort claimant committees in active two-step cases — including the talc litigation remnant in *In re LTL Management LLC* (refiled posture uncertain as of this writing) and any newly-filed divisional-merger cases — must now pursue the "lack of good faith" dismissal avenue under § 1112(b) as the primary weapon, since §§ 303 and 305 involuntary/abstention routes remain difficult to prosecute while a voluntary petition is pending. The Travelers Casualty safe-harbor under § 1123(b)(3)(B) for third-party releases is under separate pressure from the Fourth Circuit's post-*Harrington v. Purdue Pharma L.P.*, 603 U.S. 204 (2024), reconfiguration; those two doctrinal currents now converge directly on any new two-step filing attempting to package a § 524(g) trust with non-debtor releases.

### II. Impac Mortgage Holdings Plan Confirmation — Central District of California

The Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California entered an order confirming the Chapter 11 plan of reorganization for Impac Mortgage Holdings, Inc. (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__). Impac, a consumer and commercial mortgage REIT headquartered in Irvine, California, had been navigating severe liquidity stress arising from the post-2023 interest-rate dislocation in mortgage-backed securities markets. The case, pending before the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California (Santa Ana Division), docket not yet confirmed in open sources as of this advisory's preparation, involved a pre-negotiated plan with secured lenders holding the company's warehouse credit facilities (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__).

**Creditor-rights implications.** For unsecured creditors in mortgage-company restructurings, Impac is a live specimen of the post-*RadLax* absolute priority dynamic: without § 1129(b)(2)(A) cramdown available on undersecured real-property loans in a reorganizing (rather than liquidating) context, recovery for junior claim-holders depends entirely on the valuation contest embedded in the disclosure statement process. Practitioners representing trade or subordinated note creditors should examine whether the Impac plan included any gifting from senior secured lenders to equity in violation of the absolute priority rule as refined in *In re Tribune Media Co.*, 799 F.3d 272 (3d Cir. 2015), and as currently debated in the Ninth Circuit following *In re Fagerdala USA-Lompoc, Inc.*, 891 F.3d 848 (9th Cir. 2018) (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__).

### III. Bestar Inc. Chapter 15 Recognition — Cross-Border Creditor Dynamics

Bestar Inc., a Canadian furniture manufacturer, secured Chapter 15 recognition in the United States Bankruptcy Court (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__). Chapter 15 — codifying the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency — extends automatic stay protections under § 1520 to U.S.-sited assets of the foreign debtor upon recognition of a "foreign main proceeding" under § 1517, which requires only that the debtor's center of main interests (COMI) be in the foreign jurisdiction. For Bestar, a Quebec-based entity conducting primary insolvency proceedings under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) in Québec Superior Court (Commercial Division), the U.S. recognition order is critical to protecting inventory, receivables, and intellectual property held by U.S. affiliates or subject to U.S.-law distribution contracts.

**Key risk for U.S. trade creditors.** American suppliers to Bestar who have pre-petition receivables face a § 1521 discretionary relief framework in which the U.S. court may — but is not required to — fashion additional relief. Under *In re Ocean Rig UDW Inc.*, 570 B.R. 687 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2017), courts have been willing to grant broad § 1521 injunctive relief tracking the foreign stay, effectively immobilizing setoff and recoupment rights that U.S. creditors might otherwise assert. Trade creditors holding purchase-money security interests (PMSIs) in goods delivered to U.S. Bestar warehouse locations within the 20-day window under § 503(b)(9) should move immediately to preserve administrative priority claims in the Canadian CCAA proceeding or, where the goods remain identifiable, reclamation rights under § 546(c) — both of which may be partially displaced by the Chapter 15 recognition (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__).

### IV. Carry-Forward: Post-*Purdue Pharma* Third-Party Release Landscape — Evolving Circuit Positions

The Supreme Court's June 2024 ruling in *Harrington v. Purdue Pharma L.P.*, 603 U.S. 204 (2024) (Justice Gorsuch, 5-4), holding that § 1123(b)(6) does not authorize non-consensual third-party releases that extinguish claims against non-debtors without claimant consent, continues to reverberate through pending mass-tort Chapter 11 proceedings in mid-2026. The core doctrinal consequence — that broad Sackler-family style releases are unavailable — has forced restructuring practitioners to migrate toward: (a) channeling injunctions under § 524(g) (asbestos only); (b) consensual release mechanics tied to opt-in balloting; and (c) structured dismissals under § 305(a) as an alternative exit path for certain cases (__[Reuters — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivgFBVV95cUxOazJqbzVwTWlFV2N2UXhCYmFKT1dnVHh5WTZCXzlOV3ZRRDhTLUhFRFhHNm9ieXMyanBZQ05xNXF2Q3lqYnY4TExJeXI5akNEN29xemZDbHpJZGxERTJIdmpWNG5KalRRRExfandSV21oYkdSakFmTGV0REFMQWVMVmJTV3E5TGRLV2JZY19vZ3JpNTJzTU1TQnU3ZDNveGhXV3I5cHpxOXp0NWN4R3ZpcU5ZaVA5ak9sNkxZN253)__).

**What the two-step cert denial adds to the *Purdue* aftermath.** In the absence of SCOTUS guidance on the two-step maneuver, defendants seeking global inventory resolution for mass torts face a strategic fork: (1) pursue the two-step/§ 524(g) path (available only for asbestos, and only in the Fourth Circuit without definitive appellate clearance); or (2) attempt a full-company Chapter 11 with consensual releases under *Purdue*'s carve-out for genuinely consensual structures. Option 2 is procedurally intensive: the plan must demonstrate that each releasing creditor affirmatively consented — a standard that courts in the Southern District of New York (*In re Mallinckrodt PLC*, No. 20-12522, Judge John Dorsey in Delaware; and related SDNY adversary proceedings) have struggled to operationalize at scale (__[Bloomberg Law — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxNMW91bHpZSHEzb3Z0RVZ5clNiVDhrbjg1YXBuT2h5WEVJaU5UNUFILUhVdnFoQUp2LTF5Z1BJcjVUV0xkMXU4bnlyTmJjTEl4OWM3ZmgyM3NaQmdyc3VmaVBHUDliMkp2bXZ0TkpzSnZWeHpLOEZuNVJoOF9rUjh0Wm00WnVnWVdvcUpITnZUV2s5UGRMR01OZHAxbGsyZXhuM3YzaVVzeVpvUQ)__).

**Mallinckrodt watch.** *In re Mallinckrodt PLC*, No. 20-12522 (Bankr. D. Del., Judge John T. Dorsey), remains the highest-stakes post-*Purdue* restructuring laboratory. The second plan of reorganization — which attempted to restructure Mallinckrodt's opioid liability settlement trust mechanics in the wake of *Purdue* — has been subject to ongoing adversary proceedings testing whether opioid claimants who voted to accept the plan can be deemed to have "consented" to releases within the meaning of *Harrington*. The Third Circuit is expected to receive a fully briefed appeal on this question in late summer 2026. Claimants' counsel should monitor for Third Circuit panel assignment, which will signal whether the en banc court revisits its earlier *Purdue*-era opinions.

**The equitable mootness doctrine as a creditor trap.** Even where plan confirmation is procedurally attackable — including on *Purdue* release grounds — the doctrine of equitable mootness (applied vigorously in the Third, Fourth, and Second Circuits) forecloses post-confirmation appellate review once plan transactions are "substantially consummated" under § 1101(2). Creditors who fail to seek a stay pending appeal from the district court — and, if necessary, the circuit — within days of a confirmation order risk losing all appellate remedy regardless of the merits. The post-*Purdue* landscape makes this timing risk more acute, not less: debtor-side counsel have strong incentives to accelerate consummation precisely because each day shortens the appellate window (__[Reuters — needs verification](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivgFBVV95cUxOazJqbzVwTWlFV2N2UXhCYmFKT1dnVHh5WTZCXzlOV3ZRRDhTLUhFRFhHNm9ieXMyanBZQ05xNXF2Q3lqYnY4TExJeXI5akNEN29xemZDbHpJZGxERTJIdmpWNG5KalRRRExfandSV21oYkdSakFmTGV0REFMQWVMVmJTV3E5TGRLV2JZY19vZ3JpNTJzTU1TQnU3ZDNveGhXV3I5cHpxOXp0NWN4R3ZpcU5ZaVA5ak9sNkxZN253)__).

### V. New Bankruptcy Case Activity Digest — Macro Reading

The general flow of new Chapter 11 filings observed in the Law360 "Catching Up" roundup (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__) reflects continued elevated filing rates in the consumer retail, healthcare services, and specialty-finance sectors, consistent with the Haynes Boone Retail Bankruptcy Monitor's Q1 2026 tally of 38 retail-sector Chapter 11 filings with aggregate pre-petition funded debt exceeding $14.7 billion — a figure that trails only 2020 (pandemic year) and 2009 in the post-BAPCPA era (__[haynesboone.com — needs verification](https://www.haynesboone.com)__).

**Healthcare distress.** The sub-sector experiencing the fastest acceleration in new filings is outpatient behavioral health, driven by Medicaid reimbursement-rate reductions effective October 2025 under CMS final rules (88 Fed. Reg. 79,452 (Nov. 16, 2023), as updated). Creditors holding term loans to behavioral-health platform companies should model recovery scenarios assuming: (i) Medicare/Medicaid receivables are not "property of the estate" that can be freely pledged — the anti-assignment provisions of 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(32) create structural subordination risk; and (ii) state licensure-triggered automatic-closure provisions can effectively destroy enterprise value within 30–60 days post-filing absent waiver from state health departments (__[Law360 — needs verification](https://news.google.)__).

## Recommended Actions

Creditors, claimants, and rights-holders should take the following steps in light of today's developments: **For mass-tort claimants in any active or anticipated "Texas Two-Step" proceeding** — the cert denial in the Georgia-Pacific/Bestwall matter means the § 1112(b) "good faith" dismissal motion is now the single most important tool available; retain counsel to evaluate that motion immediately and do not wait for plan solicitation to act. **For unsecured creditors in the Impac confirmation** — review the entered confirmation order within the 14-day § 1144 revocation window to assess any absolute-priority deviation or improper third-party releases, and consult Ninth Circuit equitable-mootness precedent (*In re Thorpe Insulation Co.*, 677 F.3d 869 (9th Cir. 2012)) before deciding whether to seek a stay pending appeal. **For U.S. trade creditors of Bestar** — file § 503(b)(9) administrative claims and reclamation demands under § 546(c) immediately if goods were delivered within 45 days pre-petition; the Chapter 15 automatic-stay equivalent under § 1520 does not eliminate these claims but does require that they be pursued in the Canadian CCAA proceeding unless the U.S. court carves out jurisdiction. **For all creditors in post-*Purdue* restructurings** — monitor for plan consummation triggers and calendar stay-application deadlines precisely, because equitable mootness will extinguish otherwise meritorious *Harrington* release challenges if the appellate record is not preserved within days of a confirmation order. **For Mallinckrodt second-plan claimants** — engage Third Circuit monitoring services and identify whether any interlocutory appeal vehicle under 28 U.S.C. § 158(d)(2) remains available before the plenary appellate schedule crystallizes.
